items.stem: Using a horizontal force F, a table is moved across the floor at a constant velocity. How much is the frictional force exerted by the floor on the table?
items.answer: Since the table is moving at a constant velocity, the net force acting on it is zero. Therefore, the frictional force exerted by the floor on the table must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the applied horizontal force F.

items.stem: For a ball moving on a smooth frictionless surface, choose the appropriate option that will make the following statements physically correct. (i) If no net force is applied on the ball, the velocity of the ball will remain the same/increase/decrease. (ii) If a net force is applied on the ball in the direction of its motion, the magnitude of the velocity of the ball will remain the same/increase/decrease. (iii) If a net force is applied on the ball in a direction opposite to the direction of its motion, the magnitude of the velocity of the ball will remain the same/increase/decrease.
items.answer: (i) remain the same. According to Newton’s first law of motion, an object in motion will continue to move with a constant velocity unless acted upon by a net external force. (ii) increase. A net force applied in the direction of motion provides an acceleration in the same direction, causing the velocity to increase. (iii) decrease. A net force applied opposite to the motion causes deceleration, which reduces the magnitude of the ball’s velocity.

items.stem: Two blocks P and Q on a smooth horizontal surface are shown in Figure (a) and Figure (b). Two forces of magnitudes 4 N and 5 N are acting in opposite directions on block P, while block Q is moving with a constant velocity. Which of the following statement is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: (i) P experiences a net force and Q does not experience a net force.

options.label: B
options.text: (ii) P does not experience a net force and Q experiences a net force.

options.label: C
options.text: (iii) Both P and Q experience a net force.

options.label: D
options.text: (iv) Neither P nor Q experiences a net force.

items.answer: Option (i) is correct. Block P experiences unbalanced forces (5 N right and 4 N left), resulting in a net force of 1 N. Block Q is moving with constant velocity, which implies its acceleration is zero, so it experiences zero net force according to Newton’s first law.

items.stem: While practising for the snake boat race (Vallum kalli in Kerala), 100 oarsmen are rowing a boat together. Out of these, 95 row backwards to propel the boat forward. But by mistake, 5 oarsmen row in the opposite direction. If each oarsman applies a horizontal force of 200 N, what is the net force on the snake boat? (Ignore drag forces, air friction, etc.)
items.answer: The 95 oarsmen rowing backwards propel the boat forward with a total force = 95 × 200 N = 19,000 N. The 5 mistaken oarsmen row forwards, pushing the boat backwards with a total force = 5 × 200 N = 1,000 N. The net force acting on the snake boat = 19,000 N - 1,000 N = 18,000 N in the forward direction.

items.stem: When a net force acts on an object, we observe that the object accelerates:

options.label: A
options.text: (i) opposite to the direction of force, with acceleration proportional to the force acting on the object.

options.label: B
options.text: (ii) opposite to the direction of force, with acceleration proportional to the mass of the object.

options.label: C
options.text: (iii) in the direction of force, with acceleration inversely proportional to the force acting on the object.

options.label: D
options.text: (iv) in the direction of force, with acceleration proportional to the force acting on the object.

items.answer: Option (iv) is correct. According to Newton’s second law of motion, the acceleration of an object is in the direction of the net force and its magnitude is directly proportional to the net force applied.

items.stem: The position-time graph for four objects A, B, C and D moving along a straight line are given in Figure. A net force acts on:
items.answer: Option (iii) is correct. Object C has a curved position-time graph, indicating that its velocity is changing over time. A changing velocity means the object is accelerating, which requires a net force to be acting on it.

items.stem: A sailor jumps out from a small boat to the shore (Fig). As the sailor jumps forward, will the boat move? If yes, in which direction and why.
items.answer: Yes, the boat will move backward, away from the shore. According to Newton’s third law of motion, as the sailor pushes the boat backward with their feet to jump forward, the boat exerts an equal and opposite force forward on the sailor. This backward force applied by the sailor causes the boat to move in the reverse direction.

items.stem: During a high jump event, a landing mat or sand bed is placed for the athlete to fall upon (Figure). Explain the reason behind it.
items.answer: The landing mat or sand bed provides a soft, compressible surface that increases the time it takes for the falling athlete to come to a complete stop. According to Newton’s second law of motion, force is equal to the rate of change of momentum. By extending the stopping time, the rate of change of momentum decreases, which significantly reduces the impact force exerted on the athlete’s body, thereby preventing serious injuries.
items.concept: Longer impact time lowers stopping force

items.stem: A hand cart loaded with vegetables collides with an identical but empty hand cart. During the collision:

options.label: A
options.text: (i) the loaded cart exerts a force of larger magnitude on the empty cart.

options.label: B
options.text: (ii) the empty cart exerts a force of larger magnitude on the loaded cart.

options.label: C
options.text: (iii) neither cart exerts a force on the other.

options.label: D
options.text: (iv) the loaded cart and the empty cart, both exert an equal magnitude of force on each other.

items.answer: Option (iv) is correct. Newton’s third law of motion states that for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction; hence, regardless of their different masses, both carts exert an equal magnitude of force on each other during the collision.

items.stem: The acceleration-mass graph for the acceleration produced by a force on objects of different masses is plotted in the figure. The curve passes through the points (1 kg, 10 m/s²), (2 kg, 5 m/s²) and (4 kg, 2.5 m/s²). Plot the force-mass graph for this case.
items.answer: From the given graph, as the mass increases the acceleration decreases, an inverse relationship. Reading the key points off the curve and multiplying mass by acceleration: for 1 kg and 10 m/s² the force is 10 N; for 2 kg and 5 m/s² the force is 10 N; for 4 kg and 2.5 m/s² the force is again 10 N. The product of mass and acceleration is the same at every point, so the applied force is constant at 10 N. The force-mass graph is therefore a straight horizontal line parallel to the mass axis, drawn at the 10 N level.

items.stem: The velocity-time graph of an object of mass 10 kg moving along a straight line is shown in the figure. The graph is a straight line rising from 10 m/s at the start to 30 m/s at 8 s. Calculate the force acting on the object by using the graph.
items.answer: From the given graph the initial velocity is 10 m/s at the start and the final velocity is 30 m/s at 8 s. The acceleration is the change in velocity divided by the time taken, that is (30 m/s - 10 m/s) divided by 8 s, which is 20/8 or 2.5 m/s². Using Newton’s second law, force is mass multiplied by acceleration, so the force is 10 kg times 2.5 m/s². The force acting on the object is 25 N.

items.stem: A bullet of mass 50 g moving with a speed of 100 m/s enters a heavy stationary wooden block and stops after penetrating a distance of 50 cm. Estimate the stopping force acting on the bullet (assume that the bullet undergoes constant acceleration within the block).
items.answer: Given: mass of the bullet is 50 g, that is 0.05 kg; initial velocity is 100 m/s; final velocity is 0 m/s since it stops; distance is 50 cm, that is 0.5 m. Using the kinematic equation in which the square of the final velocity minus the square of the initial velocity equals twice the acceleration times the distance: 0 minus 10000 equals 2 times the acceleration times 0.5 m, so the acceleration is -10000 m/s². By Newton’s second law the force is mass multiplied by acceleration, 0.05 kg times -10000 m/s², which is -500 N. The stopping force acting on the bullet is 500 N, directed opposite to its motion.

items.stem: An ace footballer converted a penalty shot by kicking the football with a speed of 108 km h-1. The estimated force they imparted was 800 N. The mass of the football was 0.4 kg. Calculate the time of contact between their foot and the ball.
items.answer: Final velocity (v) = 108 km/h = 108 × (5/18) m/s = 30 m/s. Assuming the ball started from rest, initial velocity (u) = 0 m/s. Force (F) = 800 N. Mass (m) = 0.4 kg. Using Newton’s second law to find acceleration (a): F = ma, so a = F/m = 800/0.4 = 2000 m/s². Now, using the equation v = u + at, we get 30 = 0 + 2000 × t, t = 30/2000 = 0.015 s. The time of contact between the foot and the ball is 0.015 seconds.

items.stem: An object of mass 2 kg moving with a constant velocity of 10 m s-1 encounters a rough patch where the force of friction on the object is 7 N. At the same time, an additional constant force of 3 N opposing the motion is applied on the object. After entering the rough patch, how much distance does the object travel before coming to rest?
items.answer: Given: mass m = 2 kg; initial velocity u = 10 m s-1; final velocity v = 0 m s-1, since it comes to rest; force of friction f = 7 N opposing the motion; additional opposing force F = 3 N, also opposing the motion. Both forces act opposite to the direction of motion, so they add up: Fnet = -(f + F) = -(7 + 3) = -10 N. Using Newton’s second law, the acceleration is a = Fnet/m = -10/2 = -5 m s-2, a deceleration. Using the equation of motion v² = u² + 2as, the distance is s = (v² - u²)/(2a) = (0 - 100)/(2 × -5) = -100/-10 = 10 m. The object travels 10 m before coming to rest.

items.stem: A tractor pulls a harrow (a ploughing tool) of mass m1 with a net force F resulting in an acceleration of a1. The same tractor pulls a trolley of mass m2 with a force F producing an acceleration of a2. If the tractor now pulls the trolley with the harrow placed on it (with the same force F), then obtain an expression for the resulting acceleration in terms of a1 and a2. Ignore friction.
items.answer: From Newton’s second law, for the harrow: m1 = F/a1. For the trolley: m2 = F/a2. When they are pulled together, the combined mass is m = m1 + m2. Substituting the values of m1 and m2: m = (F/a1) + (F/a2) = F(1/a1 + 1/a2) = F[(a1 + a2)/(a1 × a2)]. The resulting acceleration (a) when force F is applied to this combined mass is: a = F/m; a = F/{F[(a1 + a2)/(a1 × a2)]}. The F cancels out, leaving: a = (a1 × a2)/(a1 + a2).

items.stem: When the pole of a bar magnet is brought close to a magnetic compass, the bar magnet and the compass needle (which is also a magnet) exert a magnetic force on each other. As per Newton’s third law of motion, both the forces are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction. However, the compass needle moves, whereas the bar magnet does not move. Explain why.
items.answer: Even though the forces acting on both the bar magnet and the compass needle are equal in magnitude, their effects are very different due to their masses. According to Newton’s second law, acceleration is inversely proportional to mass (a = F/m). The compass needle has a very tiny mass, so the magnetic force causes a large, noticeable acceleration. In contrast, the bar magnet is significantly heavier, so the same magnitude of force produces an acceleration that is too small to be noticed, and often not enough to overcome the force of static friction holding it in place.
